title: The Order in the Rocks
principle: The rocks come in layers, and the layers always come in the same order.

t: Dig straight down through the rock. The animals you find change as you go, and they change in the same order everywhere.
Drill anywhere in the world and the fossils change as you go down — and the sequence you meet is the same sequence, on every continent.
sub: Nobody arranged them. That is what makes it worth explaining.
The ordering is the fact. What produced it is the question.

question: Down at the very bottom, what kind of things do you find?
In the deepest fossil-bearing layers, what turns up?
options: Tiny simple things in the sea
stages.outcome: Tiny simple things in the sea
note: Commit. Then note which of the other two options each account below would have predicted.

t: The rocks come in layers, and the layers always come in the same order. That is called the fossil record.
Layered rock preserves a sequence, and the sequence is consistent worldwide. This is the fossil record — and the consistency, not the fossils themselves, is the thing to explain.
The geological column: a globally consistent superposition of assemblages. No single site contains all of it, but the relative order is the same wherever overlapping sections are compared.

The column is a correlation, not a stack anyone has walked down. Its force comes from the consistency of relative order across thousands of non-overlapping sections, established by index fossils long before any absolute dating existed.
sub: You never find a rabbit at the bottom.
There are no mammals in the deepest layers, anywhere, ever — and that absence is a standing invitation to falsify the whole scheme.
Haldane's challenge — 'rabbits in the Precambrian' — remains the cleanest falsification test on offer, and it has not been met.
The pattern is a forbidden-outcome claim rather than a merely accommodating one, which is what makes it scientifically interesting regardless of what one concludes about its cause.

t: The layers are real and the order is real. Here is what each side says put them there.
The stratigraphic order is agreed by everyone. The mechanism and the timescale are not.
evidence: There really are layers, they really do come in a consistent order, and there really are no mammals in the deepest ones.
Superposition, global consistency of relative order, and the absence of derived groups from lower assemblages are agreed on all sides. So are the isotope measurements taken from the rock.

claim: The layers built up slowly over a very long time, and the order is the order things lived in.
The column records deposition over roughly four billion years, and fossil order reflects the order in which groups existed.
because: Lots of separate clocks agree: rocks, ice layers, tree rings, coral bands and the light from distant stars all give the same kind of huge numbers.

Multiple independent methods converge — several radiometric systems with different half-lives and chemistries, annual ice layers counted to ~800,000, varves, coral growth bands, seafloor spreading rates, and astronomical distances. They also point to features that need long quiet intervals: buried forests with successive root systems, deep reefs grown in place, and thick evaporite beds.
predicts: New dating methods should keep giving the same huge ages, and no animal should ever turn up in the wrong layer.
Isochron and concordia methods should keep agreeing, magnetostratigraphy should keep matching, and no clearly derived group should appear below its first occurrence anywhere on earth.

claim: Most of the layers were laid down fast, in one enormous flood, only thousands of years ago.
The bulk of the fossil-bearing column was deposited rapidly during a single global Flood a few thousand years ago; the order reflects burial sequence rather than elapsed time.
because: In a huge flood, sea creatures get buried first because they are lowest, and animals that could run get buried last. They also point to fossils standing upright through many layers, which cannot have taken thousands of years.

They argue the order reflects ecological zonation, differential mobility and hydrodynamic sorting rather than succession in time, and cite rapid deposition markers: polystrate tree trunks crossing many strata, extensive flat contacts without erosion, preserved soft tissue and original proteins in dinosaur bone, and detectable carbon-14 in samples said to be far older than its half-life allows.
predicts: Layers should show signs of being laid down quickly, and things that rot fast should sometimes survive.

Rapid-deposition signatures should be widespread, short-lived molecules should keep appearing in deep strata, and the sorting should track ecological habitat and mobility rather than any independent time signal.

ask: One says the order is time. The other says the order is how things got buried. What could you dig up that would tell them apart?

The accounts make different demands. Sorting by mobility and habitat predicts one pattern; succession in time predicts another — and the two come apart for organisms that could neither flee nor float, such as pollen, plants and burrowing animals. Ask what each side accepts as the strongest evidence against its own view, and whether it has one.

q: What is the surprising thing about the fossil layers?
What is the feature of the fossil record that most needs explaining?
Which feature of the record carries the explanatory burden?
options: The order is the same all over the world
There are a lot of fossils
why: Fossils being common is not surprising. The same order turning up on every continent is — that is a pattern, and patterns need a reason.
Abundance is unremarkable; consistency of sequence across independent sites is not. A pattern that could easily have come out otherwise and did not is the thing an account has to earn.

Global consistency of relative order is the explanandum, because it is highly specific and would have been easy to violate. Both accounts on offer are attempts to supply a sorting mechanism for it, and both should be judged on how much they forbid.

t: Oil companies find oil by knowing which layer they are in. The fossils tell them.
Index fossils are working infrastructure: petroleum geology locates reservoirs by correlating strata between wells, and it does so using the same sequence, whatever anyone concludes about its age.
